claim: MELK is a serine/threonine kinase in the adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-related kinase family.
source: Maternal embryonic leucine zipper kinase (MELK) is a serine/threonine kinase in the adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-related kinase family, and was first identified as a maternal gene in mouse eggs and preimplantation embryos (Heyer et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Heyer et al., 1997 and established scientific knowledge about kinase classification.

claim: MELK was first identified as a maternal gene in mouse eggs and preimplantation embryos.
source: Maternal embryonic leucine zipper kinase (MELK) is a serine/threonine kinase in the adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-related kinase family, and was first identified as a maternal gene in mouse eggs and preimplantation embryos (Heyer et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Heyer et al., 1997.

claim: Overexpression of MELK has been reported in breast cancer.
source: In the past decade, multiple studies have reported overexpression of MELK in various cancers, including breast (Lin et al., 2007), brain (Marie et al., 2008; Nakano et al., 2008), colorectal, lung and ovarian (Gray et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al., 2007.

claim: OTSSP167 has broad-spectrum efficacy in in vitro and in vivo tumor models of various tissue origins.

claim: MELK-T1 inhibits Flt3 with an IC50 of 18 nM.

evidence: Supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2015.

claim: NVS-MELK8a exhibited high selectivity with only 7 off-target kinases inhibited >85% when profiled against 456 kinases at 1 μM.

claim: Small molecule inhibition of MELK did not significantly affect cellular growth in common culture conditions.
source: In common culture conditions, we found that small molecule inhibition, genetic deletion, or acute depletion of MELK did not significantly affect cellular growth.
evidence: Supported by data from proliferation assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Genetic deletion of MELK did not significantly affect cellular growth in common culture conditions.
source: In common culture conditions, we found that small molecule inhibition, genetic deletion, or acute depletion of MELK did not significantly affect cellular growth.
evidence: Supported by data from CRISPR/Cas9 knockout experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Acute depletion of MELK did not significantly affect cellular growth in common culture conditions.
source: In common culture conditions, we found that small molecule inhibition, genetic deletion, or acute depletion of MELK did not significantly affect cellular growth.

claim: OTSSP167 has selectivity issues.
source: This discrepancy to previous findings illuminated selectivity issues of the widely used MELK inhibitor OTSSP167, and potential off-target effects of MELK-targeting short hairpins.
evidence: Supported by kinase profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MELK-targeting short hairpins have potential off-target effects.
source: This discrepancy to previous findings illuminated selectivity issues of the widely used MELK inhibitor OTSSP167, and potential off-target effects of MELK-targeting short hairpins.
evidence: Supported by data showing that shRNAs impair growth in MELK-/- cells.

claim: JW-7-25-1 inhibits MELK with an IC50 of 5.0 nM in the Z'-LYTE enzymatic assay.
source: Its affinity for MELK was confirmed using the Z'-LYTE enzymatic assay ([ATP]=25 μM near Km of MELK), with a measured IC50 value of 5.0 nM (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by biochemical assay data presented in Table 1.

claim: HTH-01-091 inhibits MELK with an IC50 value of 10.5 nM.
source: HTH-01-091 inhibits MELK with an IC50 value of 10.5 nM, which is comparable to MELK-T1 and NVS-MELK8a in the same enzymatic assay (Figure 1A and Table 1).
evidence: Supported by biochemical assay data presented in Table 1.

claim: HTH-01-091 exhibited reduced inhibition of select off-target kinases by 20- to 140-fold when compared with JW-7-25-1.
source: Furthermore, HTH-01-091 exhibited reduced inhibition of the select off-target kinases by 20- to 140-fold when compared with JW-7-25-1 (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by biochemical assay data presented in Table 1.

claim: HTH-01-091 exhibited a greatly improved S(35) score of 0.16 at 1 μM.
source: Specifically, HTH-01-091 exhibited a greatly improved S(35) score of 0.16 at 1 μM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by KINOMEscan data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 1 μM of HTH-01-091 selectively inhibits 4% of the kinases over 90% in the ICKP panel.
source: Consistent with our previous result, 1 μM of HTH-01-091 selectively inhibits 4% of the kinases over 90%, whereas 1 μM of OTSSP167 inhibits 67% of the kinases over 90% (Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by ICKP kinase profiling data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: 1 μM of OTSSP167 inhibits 67% of the kinases over 90% in the ICKP panel.
source: Consistent with our previous result, 1 μM of HTH-01-091 selectively inhibits 4% of the kinases over 90%, whereas 1 μM of OTSSP167 inhibits 67% of the kinases over 90% (Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by ICKP kinase profiling data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: HTH-01-091 inhibited MELK activity with an IC50 value of 15.3 nM in the radioactive filter-binding assay.
source: Using the radioactive filter-binding assay provided by ICKP (Hastie et al., 2006), we found that HTH-01-091 inhibited MELK activity with an IC50 value of 15.3 nM, in good agreement with the Z'-LYTE assay, while those potential off-target kinases exhibited IC50 values in the range of 42–109 nM (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by ICKP radioactive filter-binding assay data presented in Table 2.

claim: The crystal structure of MELK in complex with HTH-01-091 revealed a type I binding mode.
source: The 2.5 Å structure of MELK in complex with HTH-01-091 revealed a type I binding mode (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data presented in Figure 1C and described in the text.

claim: The quinoline nitrogen in the tricylic core of HTH-01-091 forms the only hinge interaction with the backbone NH of Cys89.
source: The quinoline nitrogen in the tricylic core forms the only hinge interaction with the backbone NH of Cys89.
evidence: Supported by crystal structure analysis described in the text.

claim: The MRT199665 structure revealed a type I binding mode.
source: The MRT199665 structure also revealed a type I binding mode (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data presented in Figure 1D and described in the text.

claim: HTH-01-091 is cell permeable and binds to MELK in an ATP-competitive fashion.
source: HTH-01-091 dose-dependently decreased MELK pull-down by streptavidin beads, demonstrating that the compound is cell permeable and binds to MELK in an ATP-competitive fashion.
evidence: Supported by KiNativ assay data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: All MELK inhibitors tested reduced MELK protein levels in MDA-MB-468 cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that all MELK inhibitors we tested also reduced MELK protein levels in MDA-MB-468 cells, indicating that inhibitor-induced MELK degradation may be general to ATP-competitive MELK inhibitors (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Inhibitor-induced MELK degradation may be general to ATP-competitive MELK inhibitors.
source: Interestingly, we found that all MELK inhibitors we tested also reduced MELK protein levels in MDA-MB-468 cells, indicating that inhibitor-induced MELK degradation may be general to ATP-competitive MELK inhibitors (Figure 2B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all tested MELK inhibitors induced degradation.

claim: Inhibitor potency generally correlated with the rate and extent of MELK downregulation.
source: Inhibitor potency generally correlated with the rate and extent of MELK downregulation.
evidence: Inferred from the data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: MRT199665 induced the most rapid degradation of MELK protein despite being less potent than OTSSP167 based on biochemical IC50 values.
source: However, MRT199665 induced the most rapid degradation of MELK protein despite being less potent than OTSSP167 based on biochemical IC50 values.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Inhibitor-induced MELK degradation requires the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: Consistent with the prior MELK-T1 report, inhibitor-induced MELK degradation requires the ubiquitin-proteasome system, as pretreatment with the proteasome inhibitor carfilzomib prevented degradation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Beke et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to Beke et al., 2015.

claim: The cullin-RING E3 ligase family is not involved in MELK degradation.
source: However, this had minimal effect, indicating that the cullin-RING E3 ligase family is not involved in MELK degradation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data showing that MLN4924 did not prevent MELK degradation, presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: OTSSP167 demonstrated exceptional antiproliferative effects, exhibiting half maximal killing below 100 nM for most cell lines tested in 3-day proliferation assays.
source: In 3-day proliferation assays, OTSSP167 demonstrated exceptional antiproliferative effects, exhibiting half maximal killing below 100 nM for most cell lines tested (Figure 2C and Table 3).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data presented in Figure 2C and Table 3.

claim: HTH-01-091 and other selective MELK inhibitors exhibited antiproliferative IC50 values that were at least 300-fold less potent than OTSSP167.
source: In contrast, HTH-01-091 and the other selective MELK inhibitors exhibited antiproliferative IC50 values that were at least 300-fold less potent.
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data presented in Figure 2C and Table 3.

claim: MRT199665 exhibited intermediate growth inhibition in most cell lines.
source: MRT199665, which exhibited intermediate potency as a biochemical MELK inhibitor, also exhibited intermediate growth inhibition in most cell lines (Figure 2C and Table 3).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data presented in Figure 2C and Table 3.

claim: No clear difference in antiproliferative effects was observed between basal-like and luminal breast cancer subtypes in 7-day proliferation assays.
source: We evaluated the inhibitors in longer-term (7-day) proliferation assays and still observed the same trend, and no clear difference between the breast cancer subtypes (Table 4).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data presented in Table 4.

claim: The selective MELK inhibitors exhibited weak antiproliferative activities against both basal-like and luminal breast cancer cell lines in vitro.
source: In brief, the selective MELK inhibitors exhibited weak antiproliferative activities against both basal-like and luminal breast cancer cell lines in vitro, casting doubt on whether MELK inhibition affects viability.
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data presented in Tables 3 and 4.

claim: Six out of ten clones isolated from MDA-MB-468 cells transfected with Cas9/sgMELK-3 were completely deficient of MELK protein.
source: We proceeded with single cell cloning, and out of the 10 clones isolated, 6 clones were completely deficient of MELK protein, as indicated by the use of a rabbit monoclonal antibody raised against an amino-terminal epitope of MELK (EPR3981, Abcam or GeneTex) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No significant difference in growth rate was observed between WT and MELK−/− MDA-MB-468 cells.
source: We compared a WT clone (clone E9) and a MELK−/− clone (clone C7) with the parental cell line, and observed no significant difference in growth rate or cell cycle distribution (Figure 3A,B,C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: No significant difference in cell cycle distribution was observed between WT and MELK−/− MDA-MB-468 cells.
source: We compared a WT clone (clone E9) and a MELK−/− clone (clone C7) with the parental cell line, and observed no significant difference in growth rate or cell cycle distribution (Figure 3A,B,C).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: No differences in cell viability were observed between WT and MELK−/− cells after treatment with OTSSP167 or any of the more selective MELK inhibitors.
source: However, we did not observe differences in cell viability after treatment with OTSSP167 or any of the more selective MELK inhibitors, indicating that the activity of MELK inhibitors in MDA-MB-468 cells was driven by inhibition of targets other than MELK.
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: The activity of MELK inhibitors in MDA-MB-468 cells was driven by inhibition of targets other than MELK.
source: However, we did not observe differences in cell viability after treatment with OTSSP167 or any of the more selective MELK inhibitors, indicating that the activity of MELK inhibitors in MDA-MB-468 cells was driven by inhibition of targets other than MELK.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that WT and MELK-/- cells showed similar sensitivity to inhibitors.

claim: All four dTAG molecules efficiently depleted FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) within 4 hours.
source: All four degraders efficiently depleted FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) within 4 hours (Figure 4B); in particular, dTAG-13, 36, and 47 demonstrated sustained degradation of FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) for up to 72 hours (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: dTAG-13, 36, and 47 demonstrated sustained degradation of FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) for up to 72 hours.
source: All four degraders efficiently depleted FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) within 4 hours (Figure 4B); in particular, dTAG-13, 36, and 47 demonstrated sustained degradation of FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) for up to 72 hours (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Only FKBP12F36V-MELK was significantly degraded by dTAG treatment, confirming the selectivity of the system.
source: A multiplexed quantitative mass spectrometry-based proteomics experiment demonstrated that only FKBP12F36V-MELK was significantly degraded, confirming the selectivity of the system (Figure 4D) (McAlister et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data presented in Figure 4D and citation to McAlister et al., 2012.

claim: Neither of the FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) MELK−/− clones exhibited growth impairment when treated by dTAG-47 in a 9-day proliferation assay.
source: In a 9-day proliferation assay, neither of the FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) MELK−/− clones exhibited growth impairment when treated by dTAG-47 (Figure 4E), confirming that MDA-MB-468 cells are not sensitive to acute and sustained loss of MELK in vitro.
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data presented in Figure 4E.

claim: MDA-MB-468 cells are not sensitive to acute and sustained loss of MELK in vitro.
source: In a 9-day proliferation assay, neither of the FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) MELK−/− clones exhibited growth impairment when treated by dTAG-47 (Figure 4E), confirming that MDA-MB-468 cells are not sensitive to acute and sustained loss of MELK in vitro.
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data presented in Figure 4E.

claim: shMELK-1 and shMELK-2 efficiently downregulated MELK mRNA and protein levels.
source: Indeed, shMELK-1 and shMELK-2 efficiently downregulated MELK mRNA and protein levels and impaired the growth of MDA-MB-468 cells (Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and immunoblot data presented in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: shMELK-1 and shMELK-2 impaired the growth of MDA-MB-468 cells.
source: Indeed, shMELK-1 and shMELK-2 efficiently downregulated MELK mRNA and protein levels and impaired the growth of MDA-MB-468 cells (Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: The MELK-targeting hairpins caused almost identical proliferation phenotypes in a MELK−/− background.
source: Indeed, the MELK-targeting hairpins caused almost identical proliferation phenotypes in a MELK−/− background (Figure 5C,D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that off-target effects may contribute to the observed growth defects.
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data presented in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Off-target effects may contribute to the observed growth defects caused by MELK-targeting hairpins.
source: Indeed, the MELK-targeting hairpins caused almost identical proliferation phenotypes in a MELK−/− background (Figure 5C,D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that off-target effects may contribute to the observed growth defects.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that shRNAs impair growth in MELK-/- cells.

claim: Seven out of eight guide sequences targeting the transcriptional start site of MELK efficiently suppressed MELK transcript levels in MDA-MB-468-KRAB-dCas9 cells.
source: We tested 8 guide sequences that target the region around the transcriptional start site of the MELK gene, and confirmed that 7 out of 8 guide sequences efficiently suppressed MELK transcript levels in MDA-MB-468-KRAB-dCas9 cells (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Doxycycline treatment of MDA-MB-468 cells that stably express KRAB-dCas9 and the doxycycline-inducible sgRNA constructs caused efficient MELK knockdown.
source: Doxycycline treatment of MDA-MB-468 cells that stably express KRAB-dCas9 and the doxycycline-inducible sgRNA constructs caused efficient MELK knockdown, which was comparable to the MELK-targeting shRNAs (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data presented in Figure 5G.

claim: No significant difference was observed between doxycycline-treated versus non-treated groups for all five sgRNAs in a 9-day proliferation assay.
source: In a 9-day proliferation assay, we did not observe a significant difference between doxycycline-treated versus non-treated groups for all five sgRNAs, suggesting that MELK expression is not required for the fitness of MDA-MB-468 cells (Figure 5H,I, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data presented in Figure 5H and 5I.

claim: MELK expression is not required for the fitness of MDA-MB-468 cells.
source: In a 9-day proliferation assay, we did not observe a significant difference between doxycycline-treated versus non-treated groups for all five sgRNAs, suggesting that MELK expression is not required for the fitness of MDA-MB-468 cells (Figure 5H,I, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CRISPRi-mediated MELK knockdown did not impair growth.

claim: Neither chemical inhibition nor genetic manipulation of MELK in breast cancer cell lines inhibited cell growth in vitro.
source: Surprisingly, our results indicate that neither chemical inhibition nor genetic manipulation of MELK in breast cancer cell lines inhibited cell growth in vitro.
evidence: Supported by data from multiple experimental approaches presented in the manuscript.

claim: Off-target mechanisms contribute to the anticancer effects of OTSSP167.
source: By confirming that OTSSP167 and the MELK-targeting hairpins present off-target effects that cause growth defects, we deduced that MELK inhibition or depletion alone is not sufficient to impede the growth of BBC cell lines, or at a minimum, of MDA-MB-468 cells.
evidence: Supported by data showing that WT and MELK-/- cells are similarly sensitive to OTSSP167.

claim: MELK inhibition or depletion alone is not sufficient to impede the growth of BBC cell lines, or at a minimum, of MDA-MB-468 cells.
source: By confirming that OTSSP167 and the MELK-targeting hairpins present off-target effects that cause growth defects, we deduced that MELK inhibition or depletion alone is not sufficient to impede the growth of BBC cell lines, or at a minimum, of MDA-MB-468 cells.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Drug-induced degradation of MELK is general to the MELK inhibitors tested.
source: We discovered that drug-induced degradation of MELK is general to the MELK inhibitors tested.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data showing that all tested inhibitors induce MELK degradation.

claim: The rate and extent of MELK degradation largely correlated with biochemical potency for MELK inhibition.
source: While the rate and extent of degradation largely correlated with biochemical potency for MELK inhibition, we noticed that different chemical scaffolds displayed different propensities for inducing degradation.
evidence: Inferred from the data presented in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Different chemical scaffolds displayed different propensities for inducing MELK degradation.
source: While the rate and extent of degradation largely correlated with biochemical potency for MELK inhibition, we noticed that different chemical scaffolds displayed different propensities for inducing degradation.
evidence: Inferred from the data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The pyrrolopyrimidine MRT199665 induced MELK degradation most efficiently.
source: Specifically, the pyrrolopyrimidine MRT199665 induced MELK degradation most efficiently.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The inhibitor-induced MELK degradation is unlikely cell-cycle dependent.
source: The inhibitor-induced MELK degradation is unlikely cell-cycle dependent because the cells were not synchronized and we observed unchanging levels of cyclin B1 when MELK level significantly decreased (data not shown).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that cyclin B1 levels remained constant during MELK degradation.

claim: MELK likely has complex functions in cells including embryonic development, maintenance of progenitor cell fate, cell cycle regulation, and potentially cancer development.
source: MELK likely has complex functions in cells including embryonic development, maintenance of progenitor cell fate, cell cycle regulation, and potentially cancer development.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Any potential dependence on MELK in cancer is not easily modeled using common cell culture conditions.
source: The results of this study suggest that any potential dependence on MELK in cancer is not easily modeled using common cell culture conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results showing no growth defects upon MELK loss in standard culture.

claim: Combined use of genetic, pharmacological and chemical genetic perturbations is required to reach conclusions regarding target dependence.
source: Another important conclusion is the recognition that none of the tools in our study are perfectly specific, including the selective inhibitors and CRISPR-based technologies. Combined use of genetic, pharmacological and chemical genetic perturbations is required to reach conclusions regarding target dependence.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion drawn from the study's approach and findings.

claim: A missense mutation (heterozygous G20V) in MELK in MDA-MB-468 line has been reported.
source: Notably, a missense mutation (heterozygous G20V) in MELK in MDA-MB-468 line has been reported (Forbes et al., 2017), which may complicate data interpretation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Forbes et al., 2017.

claim: MELK may play a crucial role for cancer maintenance in vivo, which would only manifest in more context-dependent assays.
source: With the current data, we cannot rule out the possibility that MELK may play a crucial role for cancer maintenance in vivo, which would only manifest in more context-dependent assays.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential MELK functions not tested in this study.

claim: Both RNAi and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing impair the clonogenic growth of cancer cells, but cause minimal effects on regular cell growth.
source: Using clonogenic assays, an approach to measure the capability of single cells to grow into colonies, we recently demonstrate that both RNAi and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing impair the clonogenic growth of cancer cells, but cause minimal effects on regular cell growth (Wang et al., submitted to eLife).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., submitted to eLife.

claim: JW-7-25-1 inhibited MELK pull-down by 100% at 10 μM in KINOMEscan.
source: In particular, we focused on JW-7-25-1 (Figure 1A), a benzonaphthyridinone derivative that inhibited MELK pull-down by 100% (KINOMEscan) at 10 μM.
evidence: Supported by KINOMEscan data.

claim: JW-7-25-1 exhibited a broad kinase selectivity profile with an S(35) score of 0.54 when tested at 10 μM.
source: JW-7-25-1 exhibited a broad kinase selectivity profile with an S(35) score of 0.54 when tested at 10 μM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by KINOMEscan data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: HTH-01-091 inhibited seven kinases more strongly than MELK in the ICKP panel at 1 μM.
source: HTH-01-091 (1 μM) inhibited seven kinases more strongly than MELK in the ICKP panel, which includes PIM1/2/3, RIPK2, DYRK3, smMLCK and CLK2.
evidence: Supported by ICKP kinase profiling data presented in Figure 1B and Table 2.

claim: HTH-01-091 dose-dependently decreased MELK pull-down by streptavidin beads in the KiNativ assay.
source: HTH-01-091 dose-dependently decreased MELK pull-down by streptavidin beads, demonstrating that the compound is cell permeable and binds to MELK in an ATP-competitive fashion.
evidence: Supported by KiNativ assay data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: ERK1/2 pull-down was not affected by HTH-01-091 treatment in the KiNativ assay.
source: As a control, ERK1/2 pull-down was not affected by HTH-01-091 treatment, consistent with our profiling data showing no binding affinity of HTH-01-091 to ERK1/2 (Figure 2A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by KiNativ assay data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Pretreatment with carfilzomib prevented inhibitor-induced MELK degradation.
source: Consistent with the prior MELK-T1 report, inhibitor-induced MELK degradation requires the ubiquitin-proteasome system, as pretreatment with the proteasome inhibitor carfilzomib prevented degradation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Beke et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pretreatment with MLN4924 had minimal effect on inhibitor-induced MELK degradation.
source: However, this had minimal effect, indicating that the cullin-RING E3 ligase family is not involved in MELK degradation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The MDA-MB-468 line was authenticated by short tandem repeat analysis.
source: We authenticated our MDA-MB-468 line by short tandem repeat analysis, and repeated the proliferation assays using MDA-MB-468 cells from a second source to confirm the modest antiproliferative effects of the selective inhibitors (Table 4).
evidence: Supported by STR profiling performed by DFCI Molecular Diagnostics Laboratory.

claim: sgMELK-3 presents desirable target specificity with no sequences within the human genome with 3 or less mismatches.
source: Notably, sgMELK-3 presents desirable target specificity, as there are no sequences within the human genome with 3 or less mismatches based on ZiFit Targeter (Sander et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by ZiFit Targeter analysis and citation to Sander et al., 2010.

claim: FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) was sensitive to MRT199665-induced degradation.
source: Importantly, the exogenous MELK fusion protein was still sensitive to MRT199665-induced degradation, and was stabilized and hyperphosphorylated during mitosis, suggesting that FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) is similarly regulated as endogenous MELK (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) was stabilized and hyperphosphorylated during mitosis.
source: Importantly, the exogenous MELK fusion protein was still sensitive to MRT199665-induced degradation, and was stabilized and hyperphosphorylated during mitosis, suggesting that FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) is similarly regulated as endogenous MELK (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) is similarly regulated as endogenous MELK.
source: Importantly, the exogenous MELK fusion protein was still sensitive to MRT199665-induced degradation, and was stabilized and hyperphosphorylated during mitosis, suggesting that FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) is similarly regulated as endogenous MELK (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that FKBP12F36V-MELK(sg3R) exhibits similar properties to endogenous MELK.

claim: shMELK-5 resulted in similar levels of MELK knockdown compared with shMELK-1 and 2 two days after induction.
source: Two days after induction, shMELK-5 resulted in similar levels of MELK knockdown compared with shMELK-1 and 2, while shMELK-3 and 4 induced only about 50% MELK knockdown (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and immunoblot data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: shMELK-3 and 4 induced only about 50% MELK knockdown two days after induction.
source: Two days after induction, shMELK-5 resulted in similar levels of MELK knockdown compared with shMELK-1 and 2, while shMELK-3 and 4 induced only about 50% MELK knockdown (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and immunoblot data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: shMELK-5 induced cell growth defects.
source: Similar to previous studies using the same short-hairpin sequence (Touré et al., 2016), shMELK-5 induced cell growth defects, even though the effect was milder than shMELK-1 and 2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data presented in Figure 5B and citation to Touré et al., 2016.

claim: shMELK-4 impaired the growth of MDA-MB-468 cells while shMELK-3 did not.
source: Interestingly, for the less efficient hairpins shMELK-3 and 4, shMELK-4 also impaired the growth of MDA-MB-468 cells while shMELK-3 did not, further demonstrating that different shRNAs can lead to discrepant phenotypic outcomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Different shRNAs can lead to discrepant phenotypic outcomes.
source: Interestingly, for the less efficient hairpins shMELK-3 and 4, shMELK-4 also impaired the growth of MDA-MB-468 cells while shMELK-3 did not, further demonstrating that different shRNAs can lead to discrepant phenotypic outcomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that shMELK-3 and shMELK-4 had different effects despite similar knockdown efficiency.

claim: Sustained knockdown of MELK by shMELK-3 and 5 was observed after an 8-day treatment.
source: We observed sustained knockdown of MELK by shMELK-3 and 5 after an 8-day treatment, confirming that the growing cells maintained MELK knockdown (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The potential off-target of shMELK-2 might only manifest its effect in the presence of MELK knockdown.
source: Since the previous study was able to rescue the antiproliferative activity observed for shMELK-2 using an shRNA-resistant MELK (Wang et al., 2014), we postulated that the potential off-target of shMELK-2 might only manifest its effect in the presence of MELK knockdown, a so-called 'synthetic lethal' interaction.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the discrepancy between the current study and Wang et al., 2014.

claim: It is surprising that three independent MELK-targeting hairpins all led to loss of fitness due to off-target effects.
source: Nevertheless, it is still surprising that three independent MELK-targeting hairpins all led to loss of fitness due to off-target effects.
evidence: This is an observation and commentary on the unexpected nature of the findings.

claim: The inhibitor-induced conformation upon binding of MRT199665 is more poised for the degradation response.
source: We postulate that the induced conformation upon binding of MRT199665 is more poised for the degradation response.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why MRT199665 induces degradation most efficiently.

claim: The status of MELK phosphorylation has been proposed as a mechanism that regulates its stability during mitosis.
source: The status of MELK phosphorylation has been proposed as a mechanism that regulates its stability during mitosis (Badouel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Badouel et al., 2010.
